2618-a-house-boat-on-the-styx:
John Kendrick Bangs sets this comedy on the river Styx, where Charon the ferryman, proud of his monopoly in ferriage, paddles along one pleasant Friday morning. The dead, it turns out, have formed a house boat club, and history's great shades gather for talk, gossip, and quarrels.

Shakespeare, Napoleon, and a host of famous ghosts trade jokes and settle old scores in Bangs's light, witty prose. The book is a parlor game for learned readers, full of allusions and gentle satire. It delights as a fantasy of the afterlife run like a London club, with Charon as its put upon steward.
31523-the-women-stealers-of-thrayx:
Fox B. Holden's science-fiction story The Woman-Stealers of Thrayx, given in the catalog as The Women Stealers of Thrayx, opens with an Ihelian warrior's demand, quoted in the headnote. The Ihelians do not want Earth's arms or men, but ten thousand women, and Lieutenant Mason must take them to Earth. Mason, nervous with cold apprehension, has brought his tiny Scout too close to the Rim. He has overshot entirely, placing his small crew in what the manual calls a situation of avoidable risk.

The story follows Mason's crew as they face the Ihelian demand and the consequences of their miscalculation, with scientists in a Mark VII Explorer fifteen light-days behind. Holden writes pulp adventure with a sharp premise and a hero under pressure. Readers of vintage science fiction will find a fast tale of first contact, where diplomacy fails and a small crew must improvise.
a-house-boat-on-the-styx:
John Kendrick Bangs begins on a pleasant Friday morning on the river Styx, where Charon the ferryman is congratulating himself on his monopoly in carrying the dead. Rounding a bend, he finds another craft on his river: a house-boat, anchored and occupied. His outrage opens the book, taken from the 1902 Harper edition.

The house-boat serves as a club for famous shades. Chapter titles promise Washington giving a dinner, Hamlet making a suggestion, the house committee discussing the poets, and story-tellers' night. Shakespeare, Napoleon, and other great dead argue authorship, cookery, and ladies' day with perfect club manners. Bangs's light fantasy runs on literary jokes, and it spawned a small fleet of sequels.
britannica-1911-archaeopteryx:
Archaeopteryx is a fossil animal linking birds and reptiles. Hermann von Meyer named it from a feather. That feather came from Solenhofen in Bavaria in 1861. Lithographic slate quarries yielded it there. The geological horizon is Upper Jurassic. The same year yielded a full specimen there. That specimen is now in the British Museum. Andreas Wagner named it Griphosaurus first. Owen described it as Archaeopteryx macroura.

High prices stimulated quarry owners to search. A much finer specimen appeared in 1872. Siemens bought that Berlin specimen. He presented it to the Berlin Museum. Dames wrote an excellent monograph on it. Archaeopteryx was undoubtedly a bird. It still bore many reptilian characters, though. Those characters link the two classes. It was about a rook's size. Its long tail is its obvious peculiarity. Gadow signs this palaeontological survey.
britannica-1911-onyx:
Onyx is a banded stone, a striped form of chalcedony, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. White layers take turns with layers of black, brown, or red. A stone with red or brown bands bears the name sardonyx. The name onyx may come from the Greek word for a finger nail.

Red and white zones in the stone look not unlike a nail, the entry suggests. A thin topped form used by jewel workers bears a name that means little onyx. In the Bible the Hebrew word rendered onyx is at times read as beryl in newer versions. India has long supplied the finest stones of this kind. Dealers call any fine stone of this sort an Oriental onyx, wherever it was found.
britannica-1911-oryx:
Oryx is the scientific name of a group of African antelopes, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The Greek word means a pickaxe, and it was applied to the animal from the shape of its horns. These antelopes are of large size, with long straight or curved horns borne by both sexes. They have long tufted tails, and all of them are desert animals.

The true oryx of classical writers was in all likelihood the beisa oryx of east and north east Africa. In South Africa that kind is replaced by the gemsbuck in the same group. In northern Africa the group is held by the scimitar horned oryx. In Arabia it is held by the small white oryx, the least of the kinds named. The text sends the reader to the general piece on antelopes for the full account of the family.
britannica-1911-styx:
Styx is a myth entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the river of the dead in Greek story. In the Iliad it is the one river of the world below. In the Odyssey it is joined by Cocytus and Pyriphlegethon, which flow into the chief river Acheron. Hesiod makes Styx a daughter of Ocean. He says she was the first god to aid Zeus in his war with the Titans.

As a reward, Zeus made the most solemn oath of the gods an oath by Styx. Hesiod adds a grim penalty for a false oath by its water. The god lay in a trance for a year, without speech or breath. He then spent nine years cut off from the gods. The article ends by tying myth to place. It notes a high waterfall near Nonacris in Arcadia, which later Greeks took to be the Styx itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pyx:
The pyx, from the Latin pyxis, which renders the Greek word for a boxwood receptacle, once named every vessel that held the Blessed Eucharist. This encyclopedia entry narrows the story to its most famous use. In the Middle Ages the commonest sense was the cup in which the Sacrament rested while suspended above the altar. The eleventh-century Custumal of Cluny pictures the deacon lifting the golden pyx from the dove that hung permanently over the altar.

Later usage shrank the word to a smaller vessel of gold or silver-gilt. In it the Eucharist is carried to the sick. Such vessels are sometimes flat like a watch, sometimes raised on a little stand like a miniature ciborium. Rohault de Fleury, Otte and Bumpus supply the art-historical sources, and the entry suits readers tracing how a plain boxwood word came to name a jewelled vessel of pastoral care.
